Epidemiology & Risk Factors.title: GI Cancer Epidemiology & Risk Factors
Epidemiology & Risk Factors.html:
"GI" is not one disease. It is six different radiation oncology diseases along one tube, each with its own treatment philosophy. Before a GI consult, the first question is which of the six you're dealing with, because that decides what radiation is for: curing the cancer, preparing for surgery, sparing an organ, controlling a tumor locally, or relieving symptoms.

Six Diseases, Six Treatment Identities

DiseaseCore treatment identityRadiation's usual job
AnusDefinitive chemoRT; surgery mainly for salvageThe curative treatment
RectumMRI risk stratification → TNT or RT → TME or organ preservationNeoadjuvant and risk-adapted; omitted in selected lower-risk patients
EsophagusNeoadjuvant chemoRT or chemo → surgery, or definitive chemoRTNeoadjuvant or definitive
PancreasResectability and systemic therapy come firstSelected local therapy
Liver (HCC)Liver function + tumor burden → local liver therapy, SBRT, or systemic therapyOne of several liver-directed options
StomachSurgery + systemic therapySelective: some postoperative situations and palliation
Colon cancer is intentionally not a major topic here. It is treated with surgery and systemic therapy, and radiation is rarely part of routine care.

Who Gets Which Cancer

SiteMain driversClassic presentationWhy it matters for you
EsophagusSCC: smoking, alcohol. Adeno: Barrett's, GERD, obesityProgressive dysphagia (solids, then liquids), weight lossHistology and location shape the surgical versus definitive chemoRT decision
StomachH. pylori, smoked/salted foods, CDH1 (hereditary diffuse type)Early satiety, weight loss, anemia, bleedingSurgery-led; RT is selective
PancreasSmoking, chronic pancreatitis, long-standing diabetes, obesity; BRCA1/2, PALB2, LynchPainless jaundice (head), back pain and weight loss (body/tail), new-onset diabetesUsually found late, so systemic therapy leads
Liver (HCC)Cirrhosis: hepatitis B/C, alcohol, MASLD/MASH (hepatitis B can cause HCC without cirrhosis)Often found on surveillance; sometimes decompensationLiver function limits treatment as much as the tumor does
RectumAge, IBD, Lynch, FAP; rising in young adultsRectal bleeding, change in bowel habits, tenesmusMRI and tumor height decide the plan; MMR status can change it
AnusHPV, HIV and other immunosuppression, smoking, prior HPV-related dysplasiaBleeding, pain, a mass; often blamed on hemorrhoidsCured with chemoRT in most patients
Pancreatic cancer is relatively uncommon but disproportionately lethal, because it is usually diagnosed late.

Esophageal Cancer: Two Diseases in One Organ

Both present with progressive dysphagia and weight loss, but the two histologies behave like different diseases sharing one organ:

Squamous cell (SCC)
Upper/mid esophagus

Linked to smoking and alcohol (also achalasia and caustic injury). The dominant type worldwide. More radiosensitive, so definitive chemoRT is a real option for selected patients.

Adenocarcinoma
Distal esophagus / GEJ

Linked to Barrett's, GERD, and obesity. The dominant type in the US. Perioperative systemic therapy plays a larger role.

Clinical Pearl

Location changes the plan too. A cervical esophageal tumor is treated more like a head and neck cancer, with definitive chemoRT, because surgery there would mean removing the larynx.

Rectal vs Anal: Neighbors, Different Diseases

Rectum
Adenocarcinoma
  • Sporadic, IBD, Lynch, FAP; rising in adults under 50
  • Drains mainly to mesorectal and pelvic nodes
  • MRI → risk → neoadjuvant therapy → TME or organ preservation
  • MMR-deficient tumors can respond dramatically to immunotherapy
Anus
HPV-driven squamous cell carcinoma
  • HPV, HIV, immunosuppression, smoking
  • Below the dentate line drains to the groins
  • Definitive chemoRT; surgery is salvage
  • Most patients keep their sphincter
Self-check: a 48-year-old with HIV has rectal bleeding blamed on hemorrhoids for a year. What should you worry about?▾

Anal cancer. HIV is a major risk factor, and bleeding and pain are often dismissed as hemorrhoids. Exam, anoscopy, and biopsy of any mass.

Pancreas, Liver, and Stomach: The Essentials

1
Pancreas

Painless jaundice from a head tumor; back pain and weight loss from body/tail tumors. Smoking is the main modifiable risk. Hereditary syndromes (BRCA1/2, PALB2, Lynch) matter enough that germline testing is offered to every patient.

2
Liver (HCC)

Arises in cirrhosis, so patients carry two diseases: the tumor and the liver. People with cirrhosis are screened with ultrasound, and the liver's reserve (Child-Pugh) shapes every treatment option.

3
Stomach

H. pylori drives the intestinal type; CDH1 causes hereditary diffuse gastric cancer. Treatment is surgery and systemic therapy, with radiation reserved for selected situations.

Clinical Pearl

New-onset diabetes plus unexplained weight loss in an older adult should raise suspicion for pancreatic cancer.

Reference: hereditary syndromes and screening▾
SyndromeGeneGI relevance
LynchMLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 (mismatch repair)Colorectal (MSI-high), endometrial, ovarian, gastric, pancreatic, urinary tract cancers; MMR-deficient tumors respond to immunotherapy
FAPAPCHundreds to thousands of polyps; prophylactic colectomy
Hereditary breast/ovarianBRCA1/2, PALB2Pancreatic cancer; may respond to platinum and PARP inhibitors
Other pancreatic syndromesSTK11 (Peutz-Jeghers), CDKN2A (FAMMM), PRSS1High-risk relatives may get pancreatic surveillance with EUS/MRI
Hereditary diffuse gastricCDH1Diffuse gastric and lobular breast cancer
  • Average-risk colorectal screening now starts at 45 in the US because of rising young-onset disease.
  • Patients with cirrhosis (and some with hepatitis B) get ultrasound ± AFP about every 6 months.
High-Yield Summary
  • GI is six diseases with six treatment identities: chemoradiation cures anal cancer, rectal treatment is risk-adapted around the MRI, esophageal RT is neoadjuvant or definitive, and pancreas, liver, and stomach use RT selectively.
  • Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma is upper or mid esophageal and linked to smoking and alcohol, while adenocarcinoma is distal or at the GEJ and linked to Barrett's, GERD, and obesity.
  • Pancreatic cancer classically presents with painless jaundice, back pain, or new diabetes with weight loss, and it is disproportionately lethal because it is usually found late.
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma usually arises in cirrhosis, so liver function limits treatment as much as the tumor does.
  • Rectal cancer is an adenocarcinoma, while anal cancer is an HPV-driven squamous cancer with higher risk in HIV that is often mistaken for hemorrhoids.

Anatomy & Lymphatics.title: The GI Tract: Anatomy, Levels & Lymph Nodes
Anatomy & Lymphatics.html:
GI anatomy is a trip down one long tube. At every stop, ask three things: the organ's regions (which shape the surgery and the stage), what's next to it (the organs at risk), and where it drains (which nodes go in the field). This page has two interactive modules: the organs from top to bottom and the nodal basins for each site. The axial CT levels are in the Imaging module.

The GI Tract, Top to Bottom

Esophagus

SegmentDistance from incisorsWhy it matters
Cervical15-20 cmNext to the larynx; treated more like head and neck cancer (definitive chemoRT)
Upper thoracic20-25 cmBehind the trachea; airway invasion is a concern
Middle thoracic25-30 cmBehind the left atrium; heart and lungs are the main OARs
Lower thoracic30-40 cmBarrett's and adenocarcinoma; moves with breathing
GEJ~40 cmJunction tumors may be treated as esophageal or gastric depending on where the center sits

Because the esophagus lacks a serosal barrier and has a longitudinal lymphatic network in its submucosa, microscopic disease can extend well beyond the visible tumor. That's why esophageal target volumes are long.

Planning details: esophageal CTV margins▾
  • A common approach expands the GTV about 3-4 cm superiorly and inferiorly (along the mucosa) and about 1 cm radially, trimmed off uninvolved bone, heart, and lung. CROSS used 4 cm longitudinally.
  • Distal and GEJ tumors usually extend the inferior margin along the gastric cardia and cover celiac-region nodes; upper tumors may include supraclavicular nodes.
  • Margins differ by protocol and guideline; follow the institutional or trial protocol.

Pancreas and Liver

  • Pancreas: head (with the uncinate process; most cancers; painless jaundice), neck (over the SMV/portal vein), body, tail (near the spleen).
  • Resectability depends on the vessels wrapped around it: arteries (SMA, celiac axis, common hepatic artery) and veins (SMV, portal vein). The duodenum wraps the head and is the main organ that limits pancreatic radiation dose.
  • Liver: 8 Couinaud segments; the portal vein brings most of its blood, but HCC is fed by the hepatic artery, which is why it enhances early. The dome moves with breathing.
In HCC, the organ containing the tumor is also a critical organ at risk.

Rectum and Anal Canal

Rectum
Measured from the anal verge
  • Described as low, mid, or upper (roughly 0-5, 5-10, and 10-15 cm)
  • Wrapped in the mesorectum (fat, vessels, nodes), bounded by the mesorectal fascia (MRF)
  • TME removes the mesorectum intact; the MRF is the surgical margin
  • Above the peritoneal reflection, the upper rectum behaves more like colon
  • Low tumors near the sphincter may need an APR (permanent colostomy) instead of a sphincter-saving low anterior resection
Anal canal
A short canal, ~3-4 cm
  • From the anorectal ring to the anal verge
  • The dentate line splits the drainage: above → pelvic (mesorectal/internal iliac); below → inguinal
  • Internal and external sphincters control continence
  • The anal margin is the perianal skin around the verge
In low rectal cancer, anatomy matters because the sphincter and the mesorectal planes decide whether sphincter-saving surgery or organ preservation is realistic.
Self-check: a rectal tumor's lower edge is 3 cm from the anal verge. Why does that height matter so much?▾

It's a low rectal cancer. Surgery may need an APR (permanent colostomy), and the mesorectum is thin there, so margins are harder to achieve. That makes organ preservation especially valuable, which is one reason neoadjuvant therapy is often planned with that goal in mind.

The Lymph Nodes: What Changes My Field?

Start with the nodes each primary drains to first, then ask what about this patient's tumor adds another basin.

SiteStandard nodal coverageWhat adds more
EsophagusPeriesophageal nodes along the tumor lengthUpper/cervical tumors: supraclavicular nodes. Distal/GEJ tumors: celiac and left gastric nodes
Stomach (when RT is used)Perigastric and celiac-branch nodesDriven by tumor location and the surgical findings
PancreasPeripancreatic and celiac/SMA regionElective nodal coverage varies; SBRT often treats only the tumor and the involved vessel interface
RectumMesorectal + presacral + internal iliac/obturatorExternal iliac: anterior organ invasion (bladder, prostate, vagina) or selected T4. Inguinal: anal canal involvement
AnusInguinal + mesorectal + presacral + internal and external iliacThe groins are part of the standard field
Anal cancer: the groins are regional. Rectal cancer drains mainly to mesorectal and pelvic nodes; inguinal nodes are generally nonregional, but a tumor that involves the anal canal or certain adjacent structures can change the drainage pattern and the field.

Most GI sites stage nodes by count; anal cancer stages them by location. The exact cutoffs are in the staging tables in Workup & Staging.

Planning details: rectal and anal elective nodal volumes▾
  • Rectal CTV: the tumor with margin, the entire mesorectum, and the presacral, internal iliac, and obturator nodes, usually from about the sacral promontory (or the common iliac bifurcation) down to the pelvic floor, extended below the tumor as needed.
  • Anal CTV: the primary with margin, mesorectum, presacral, internal and external iliac, and inguinal nodes; involved nodes get a higher dose than elective ones.
  • Exact boundaries come from consensus contouring atlases (for example, the RTOG anorectal atlas).
High-Yield Summary
  • The esophagus lacks a serosa and has longitudinal lymphatics, so microscopic disease can extend beyond the visible tumor and target volumes are long.
  • The mesorectal fascia is the TME surgical plane, and in low rectal cancer the sphincter and mesorectal planes decide whether sphincter-saving surgery or organ preservation is realistic.
  • The dentate line splits anal drainage, and for anal cancer the groins are regional and part of the standard field.
  • Rectal cancer drains mainly to the mesorectal, presacral, and internal iliac nodes, with external iliac nodes added for anterior organ invasion and inguinal nodes when the anal canal is involved.
  • In HCC the liver is both the organ with the tumor and the critical organ at risk, and pancreatic resectability depends on the SMA, celiac axis, common hepatic artery, and SMV/portal vein.

Imaging.title: GI Imaging: MRI, CT, EUS & PET/CT
Imaging.html:
Every imaging study should answer a clinical question. In GI that question differs by organ: how deep, how far, can it be removed, is it HCC, or how close is it to the margin? Each primary below is grouped from the esophagus down to the anus, with its normal axial anatomy first and then its key staging scans. This section comes before Workup & Staging because staging these cancers is mostly reading these studies.

SiteStudyQuestion it answers
EsophagusEUSHow deep? (T1a vs deeper; nearby nodes)
PET/CTNodes or metastases? How long is the tumor?
StomachCT ± PET; diagnostic laparoscopyIs there peritoneal disease that CT can't see?
PancreasPancreatic-protocol CTCan it be removed with a negative (R0) margin?
Liver (HCC)Multiphase CT or MRIIs this HCC? How much liver is involved?
RectumPelvic MRIT stage, margin, and spread
AnusMRILocal extent (sphincters, vagina, prostate)
PET/CTNodal and distant disease
Upper abdomen4D-CT at simulationHow much does the target move with breathing?

Esophagus

  • EUS sees the wall layers: T1a (mucosa) may be removed endoscopically; T1b and deeper need surgery or chemoRT.
  • PET/CT finds nodes and distant disease, often changes management, and helps define the tumor length for contouring.
  • Upper and mid tumors near the airway: bronchoscopy to rule out tracheal invasion or fistula.
  • Distal tumors move with breathing, so planning uses 4D-CT.
  • On the normal levels: the upper thoracic esophagus sits behind the trachea at the aortic arch; the mid esophagus sits right behind the left atrium, next to the subcarinal nodes. Organs at risk here are the spinal cord, lungs, and heart.

Stomach and GEJ

  • CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for everyone; EUS when early-stage disease is suspected; PET/CT for locally advanced disease.
  • CT misses peritoneal disease, so diagnostic laparoscopy with washings comes before curative surgery.
  • The GEJ and stomach move with breathing. Organs at risk at this level: liver, kidneys, spleen, bowel, and heart.

Pancreas

Pancreatic cancer is a surgical anatomy problem. The scan exists to answer one question: can the tumor be removed with a negative (R0) margin?

  • Thin-slice CT in arterial (pancreatic) and portal venous phases. The tumor is hypoenhancing (darker than normal pancreas).
  • Double duct sign: a dilated common bile duct and pancreatic duct point to a pancreatic head (or ampullary) mass.
  • Describe each key vessel: SMA, celiac axis, common hepatic artery, SMV, and portal vein, and whether contact is ≤180° or >180° of the circumference.
  • Get the scan before a biliary stent when possible, because stent-related inflammation blurs the tumor edge.
  • Organs at risk at this level: duodenum, stomach, bowel, kidneys, liver, and spinal cord.

Liver (HCC)

  • Arterial enhancement + washout (often with a capsule) is the HCC pattern.
  • In the appropriate at-risk patient (usually cirrhosis), a LI-RADS 5 lesion can establish the diagnosis without a biopsy.
  • Imaging also measures how much liver is involved and how much healthy liver would be left, which matters as much as the tumor.
  • Portal vein tumor thrombus signals advanced disease; it can influence treatment selection and may be amenable to liver-directed radiation in selected patients.
  • For liver SBRT: 4D-CT or breath hold (the liver moves with breathing), often fiducials for daily alignment, and contrast-enhanced planning scans.

Rectum

Rectal MRI is the single most important GI imaging study for a Rad Onc student. Read it with three questions: T, Margin, Spread.

T
How far through the wall?

Intact dark muscularis propria = T1-2. Into the mesorectal fat = T3. Through the peritoneum or into another organ = T4.

M
How close to the margin?

The distance from tumor, EMVI, deposits, or nodes to the mesorectal fascia. ≤1 mm = threatened.

S
Has it spread?

EMVI, suspicious mesorectal or lateral nodes, tumor deposits, and (on CT) distant disease.

Also note the height from the anal verge and whether the tumor reaches the sphincter.

A threatened MRF means a higher risk of local recurrence, so treatment intensification becomes more important.
  • A restaging MRI with endoscopy after neoadjuvant therapy decides whether the patient has a complete clinical response. Look for dark fibrosis without residual intermediate-signal tumor or restricted diffusion.
  • Organs at risk at this level: small bowel, bladder, and femoral heads.

Anus

  • Pelvic MRI defines local extent: sphincters, vagina, prostate.
  • PET/CT finds inguinal and pelvic nodes that CT misses, which can change the stage and the dose to nodes.
  • On CT, the inguinal nodes sit along the femoral vessels in the groin and are part of the standard anal cancer field.
  • After chemoRT, be patient: tumors keep shrinking for months, so response is judged over several months (up to about 26 weeks).
  • Organs at risk at this level: bowel, bladder, genitalia, femoral heads, and perineal skin.
Self-check: rectal MRI shows a T3 tumor with a mesorectal node 0.8 mm from the mesorectal fascia. Is the margin threatened?▾

Yes. Tumor, a node, a tumor deposit, or EMVI within 1 mm of the MRF all count. A threatened margin is a reason to intensify neoadjuvant therapy, typically TNT including long-course chemoRT.

High-Yield Summary
  • Each GI imaging study answers a question: EUS asks how deep, PET/CT asks whether there is spread, pancreatic-protocol CT asks whether the tumor can be removed, and multiphase liver imaging asks whether it is HCC.
  • Rectal MRI is read as T, Margin, and Spread, and a mesorectal fascia threatened within 1 mm raises the risk of local recurrence.
  • Pancreatic-protocol CT measures how much the tumor touches the major arteries and veins, ideally before a biliary stent is placed.
  • In an at-risk patient, arterial enhancement with washout (LI-RADS 5) can diagnose HCC without a biopsy.
  • Anal cancer keeps shrinking for months after chemoradiation, so response is judged over several months rather than right after treatment.

Workup & Staging.title: GI Cancer Workup & Staging
Workup & Staging.html:
T = depth, N = nodes, M = distant spread is the starting point, but GI has no single staging logic. Each site turns on different questions, and some (pancreas, liver) are planned around something other than TNM. Learn what actually changes management at each site; the NCCN workup and full AJCC tables are at the bottom of the page.

What Actually Decides the Plan

SiteStaging really asks aboutKey tools
EsophagusDepth + nodes + location + histologyEUS, PET/CT
StomachDepth + nodes + peritoneal diseaseCT, EUS, laparoscopy with washings
RectumMRI anatomy: T, MRF, EMVI, nodes, height; plus MMR statusPelvic MRI
PancreasResectabilityPancreatic-protocol CT, multidisciplinary review
Liver (HCC)Tumor burden + liver function + performance statusMultiphase CT/MRI, Child-Pugh, BCLC
AnusTumor size + node locationExam, MRI, PET/CT

The Usual Pattern (and the Exceptions)

T
How deep through the wall?

The wall layers repeat: mucosa → submucosa → muscularis propria → beyond the wall → adjacent organs. Anal cancer uses size instead.

N
How many nodes?

Most GI sites count regional nodes. Anal cancer uses node location instead.

M
Distant spread?

Includes nonregional nodes and, for the stomach and pancreas, positive peritoneal cytology.

The Core Workup

Almost every GI cancer gets the same backbone:

  1. History and exam: weight loss, nutrition, performance status. For anal and low rectal cancer, add DRE, anoscopy, and a groin node exam.
  2. Tissue: endoscopy with biopsy (EGD, colonoscopy, or EUS-guided for pancreas). Rectal cancer gets a full colonoscopy to find synchronous lesions.
  3. Local imaging (site-specific) plus CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; PET/CT for esophageal and anal cancer.
  4. Labs and markers: CBC, liver and kidney function; CEA (colorectal), CA 19-9 (pancreas), AFP (HCC), HIV (anal).
  5. Biomarkers: MMR/MSI for colorectal, gastric, esophageal, and pancreatic tumors; HER2 and PD-L1 for esophagogastric adenocarcinoma; germline testing for pancreatic cancer.
  6. Supportive care: nutrition (a feeding tube for obstructing esophageal tumors), smoking cessation, stoma counseling.

Esophagus

Depth (EUS) decides whether endoscopic therapy is possible; nodes (EUS, PET/CT) are counted; histology and location shape the treatment pathway. SCC and adenocarcinoma share T/N/M definitions but have separate stage groups.

FindingWhat it changes
T1a (mucosa only)Endoscopic resection may be enough
T1b-T2, N0Surgery is usually the main treatment
T3-T4a or node-positiveMultimodality therapy: neoadjuvant therapy → surgery, or definitive chemoRT
T4b (aorta, vertebra, airway)Not resectable: definitive chemoRT
Traps and high-yield
  • Celiac nodes are regional for esophageal cancer; supraclavicular nodes are generally considered distant (M1).
  • Cervical esophageal tumors are usually treated with definitive chemoRT, not surgery.
  • Junction tumors whose center sits well below the GEJ (Siewert III) are usually treated as gastric.

Stomach

Same depth and node-count logic as the esophagus, plus one extra question: is there peritoneal disease? CT misses it, so diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal washings comes before curative surgery for anything beyond very early disease. Positive peritoneal cytology is M1 (stage IV) even with no visible implants.

Pancreas: Resectability Is the Stage That Matters

TNM provides prognostic staging, but treatment planning is driven by radiographic resectability on a pancreatic-protocol CT and multidisciplinary surgical assessment. The core rule is how much the tumor touches the arteries versus the veins:

CategoryArteries (SMA, celiac, CHA)Veins (SMV, portal vein)
ResectableNo contactNo contact or limited (≤180°) contact
BorderlineLimited contact (e.g., SMA ≤180°)More extensive involvement that can still be reconstructed
Locally advancedEncasement (>180°) of the SMA or celiac axisNot reconstructable
Reference: full NCCN resectability criteria▾
CategoryArteriesVeins
ResectableNo arterial contact (celiac, SMA, CHA)No contact, or ≤180° without contour irregularity
BorderlineHead/uncinate: CHA contact without extension to the celiac or hepatic bifurcation; SMA ≤180°; variant arterial anatomy. Body/tail: celiac ≤180°, or >180° without aorta or GDA involvement>180°, or ≤180° with contour irregularity or thrombosis, but reconstructable; IVC contact
Locally advancedHead/uncinate: SMA or celiac >180°. Body/tail: SMA or celiac >180°, or celiac contact with aortic involvementUnreconstructable SMV/PV from tumor involvement or occlusion
Quick check: head tumor, SMV contact of 200° over a short segment that can be reconstructed, no arterial contact. Category?▾

Borderline resectable. Extensive venous contact that can be reconstructed. The usual plan is neoadjuvant systemic therapy (± RT), restaging, and then surgery with vein resection if feasible.

Traps and high-yield
  • Any distant metastasis, including nonregional nodes, makes the cancer unresectable regardless of vessel anatomy.
  • Locally advanced is not always permanent: a good response to systemic therapy occasionally makes surgery possible.

Liver (HCC): Tumor, Liver, and Patient

HCC treatment weighs three things at once: tumor burden, liver function (Child-Pugh: bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy), and performance status. The BCLC system combines them and links each stage to a usual treatment. TNM is mainly used for pathology after resection or transplant.

Workup adds: multiphase CT or MRI, AFP, hepatitis panel, signs of portal hypertension (varices, splenomegaly, low platelets), and chest CT. FDG-PET is not routinely used to stage HCC.

Reference: BCLC stages▾
BCLCTumor / function / PSUsual treatment
0 (very early)Single ≤2 cm, preserved function, PS 0Resection / ablation / transplant
A (early)Single, or ≤3 nodules each ≤3 cm; preserved function, PS 0Resection / ablation / transplant
B (intermediate)Multinodular, preserved function, PS 0TACE (or other liver-directed therapy); transplant in selected patients
C (advanced)Portal invasion and/or extrahepatic spread, PS 1-2Systemic therapy
D (terminal)End-stage liver function, PS 3-4Best supportive care

A large single HCC without vascular invasion can still be resected if the liver reserve allows.

Rectum: Stage on MRI

AJCC TNM still applies, but the decisive staging tool is high-resolution pelvic MRI, read as T, Margin, Spread (see Imaging). Add height and MMR status, and you can sort the patient by risk:

Features of lower risk
Locally advanced, less threatening
  • Mid or upper tumor
  • Limited extension into the mesorectal fat
  • Clear MRF
  • No EMVI; limited nodal disease
Features of higher risk
Higher recurrence risk
  • T4
  • Threatened or involved MRF
  • EMVI, tumor deposits
  • Bulky nodal disease or enlarged lateral pelvic nodes
  • Low tumor near the sphincter
Biology can override anatomy: MMR-deficient rectal cancers can respond dramatically to immunotherapy, so MMR status belongs in the first workup.
Quick check: mid-rectal T2N0, MRF clear, MMR-proficient. Does this patient need radiation?▾

Not routinely. Early rectal cancer usually goes straight to TME. Neoadjuvant therapy is considered mainly when organ preservation is a goal, as in some low tumors.

Traps and high-yield
  • EMVI and tumor deposits predict distant recurrence: don't anchor only on N.
  • Rectal staging is a risk assessment, not a single TNM cutoff that switches on one treatment.

Anus: Size and Node Location

The GI exception: T is by size and N is by node location. Workup adds DRE, anoscopy, an inguinal node exam (sample a suspicious node), MRI and CT ± PET/CT, HIV testing, and gynecologic exam with cervical screening in women.

TSizeNLocation
T1≤2 cmN1aInguinal, mesorectal, internal iliac, or obturator
T2>2-5 cmN1bExternal iliac
T3>5 cmN1cExternal iliac + any N1a
T4Invades an adjacent organ (vagina, urethra, bladder)

Stage shapes the dose and the field, not whether chemoRT is used: nearly all anal canal SCC is treated with definitive chemoRT.

Traps and high-yield
  • Sphincter or skin involvement does not make a tumor T4; only an adjacent organ does.
  • In the AJCC 9th edition, tumor size weighs more heavily than node status in the stage groups.
  • HIV status alone doesn't change the treatment in patients with good immune function.

NCCN Workup by Site

What the NCCN Esophageal/Gastric, Pancreatic, Hepatobiliary, Rectal, and Anal Carcinoma Guidelines recommend before treatment, simplified for learning. Always check the current guideline for real patients.

DiagnosisEGD + biopsy; EUS if no metastases
ImagingCT chest/abdomen with contrast; PET/CT
BiomarkersHER2 (adenocarcinoma), MMR/MSI, PD-L1
OtherBronchoscopy for tumors at/above the carina; nutrition assessment (feeding tube); surgical evaluation
DiagnosisEGD + biopsy; EUS
ImagingCT chest/abdomen/pelvis; PET/CT if no metastases
Staging surgeryLaparoscopy with peritoneal washings (T1b or higher, before resection)
BiomarkersHER2, MMR/MSI, PD-L1; H. pylori testing
ImagingPancreatic-protocol CT (or MRI), CT chest; ideally before stenting
TissueEUS-guided biopsy (needed before neoadjuvant therapy)
LabsCA 19-9 (after bilirubin normalizes), LFTs
GeneticsGermline testing for everyone; tumor molecular profiling for advanced disease
DecisionMultidisciplinary review of resectability
ImagingMultiphase CT or MRI (LI-RADS); CT chest
LabsAFP, hepatitis B/C, LFTs, INR (Child-Pugh / MELD)
BiopsyNot needed for LI-RADS 5 in cirrhosis; otherwise biopsy
DecisionTransplant / surgery / ablation / liver-directed therapy / systemic, by multidisciplinary team
EndoscopyBiopsy, full colonoscopy, rigid proctoscopy (height)
ImagingPelvic MRI (preferred) or ERUS; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis
Labs / markersCBC, chemistry, CEA, MMR/MSI
OtherStoma teaching, fertility counseling; enterostomal evaluation
ExamDRE, anoscopy, inguinal node exam (FNA if suspicious); gynecologic exam with cervical screening in women
ImagingCT chest/abdomen/pelvis ± PET/CT; pelvic MRI
LabsHIV testing (CD4 if positive)

AJCC Staging Tables

T1a / T1bLamina propria or muscularis mucosae / submucosa
T2 / T3Muscularis propria / adventitia
T4a / T4bPleura, pericardium, azygos, diaphragm, peritoneum / aorta, vertebral body, trachea
N1 / N2 / N31-2 / 3-6 / ≥7 regional nodes
M1Distant (incl. supraclavicular nodes)
T1a / T1b / T2Lamina propria / submucosa / muscularis propria
T3 / T4a / T4bSubserosa / serosa / adjacent structures
N1 / N2 / N3a / N3b1-2 / 3-6 / 7-15 / ≥16 nodes
T1 / T2 / T3≤2 cm / >2-4 cm / >4 cm
T4Involves celiac axis, SMA, and/or common hepatic artery
N1 / N21-3 / ≥4 nodes
T1 / T2Submucosa / muscularis propria
T3Through the muscularis propria into pericolorectal tissue
T4a / T4bVisceral peritoneum / invades or adheres to other organs
N1a / N1b / N1c1 node / 2-3 nodes / tumor deposits without nodes
N2a / N2b4-6 / ≥7 nodes
M1a / M1b / M1cOne organ / >1 organ / peritoneum
T1 / T2 / T3≤2 cm / >2-5 cm / >5 cm
T4Invades adjacent organs (vagina, urethra, bladder)
N1a / N1b / N1cInguinal, mesorectal, superior rectal, internal iliac, or obturator / external iliac / both
Stage groups (9th ed.)I T1N0 · IIA T2N0 · IIB T1-2N1 · IIIA T3N0-1 · IIIB T4N0 · IIIC T4N1 · IV M1
High-Yield Summary
  • GI has no single staging logic: esophagus turns on depth, nodes, location, and histology, while rectum turns on MRI anatomy and MMR status.
  • Pancreatic TNM is prognostic, but treatment planning is driven by resectability on pancreatic-protocol CT and multidisciplinary surgical review.
  • HCC treatment weighs tumor burden, liver function, and performance status together, which is what the BCLC system combines.
  • Rectal cancer is sorted by risk, and T4 disease, a threatened mesorectal fascia, EMVI, bulky or lateral nodes, or a low tumor all raise it.
  • Anal cancer is staged by tumor size and node location, and the stage shapes the dose and field rather than whether chemoradiation is used.

Treatment Paradigms.title: GI Cancer Treatment Paradigms
Treatment Paradigms.html:
In GI cancer, radiation can be definitive, neoadjuvant, selectively adjuvant, ablative, or palliative, depending on the organ, the anatomy, and the disease biology. For every consult, work through three questions:

1
Which of the six diseases?

Anus, rectum, esophagus, pancreas, liver, or stomach. Each has its own treatment identity (see Epidemiology).

2
Where does surgery stand?

Is the tumor resectable, is the patient fit for surgery, and is organ preservation a realistic goal?

3
What is radiation's job?

Cure the cancer, prepare for surgery, spare an organ, control the tumor locally, or relieve symptoms.

Anus: chemoRT is definitive and surgery is mainly salvage. At the other GI sites, radiation may be neoadjuvant, definitive, selectively adjuvant, ablative, or palliative, depending on anatomy and disease biology.

Paradigm 1: Anal Cancer: ChemoRT Is the Cure

The cleanest GI paradigm, and a favorite for Sub-I questions:

1
Biopsy-proven anal SCC
→
2
Stage, including the inguinal nodes
→
3
Definitive chemoRT
→
4
Slow response is expected: observe clinically
→
5
Biopsy persistent or progressive disease → salvage surgery
  • Concurrent 5-FU (or capecitabine) + mitomycin with IMRT and image guidance; dose is adapted to the tumor and nodal extent.
  • The field includes the pelvic and inguinal nodes in standard cases.
  • Avoid treatment breaks: prolonging treatment lowers cure rates, so skin care and supportive care matter.
  • Tumors keep shrinking for months after treatment. Residual disease that is still regressing is watched; biopsy-proven persistent or progressive disease goes to salvage APR.
  • Small, well-differentiated anal margin tumors can sometimes be treated with local excision. People with HIV and good immune function get standard therapy.
Nigro

Showed chemoRT could eradicate anal cancer without routine APR, so most patients keep their sphincter.

ACT II

Cisplatin did not beat mitomycin, maintenance chemo didn't help, and many tumors only reached complete response by about 26 weeks.

Restage: TME or watch-and-wait
  • Early (T1-2 N0): TME without radiation in most patients; local excision for selected small T1 tumors. For a low tumor where the patient wants to avoid a stoma, neoadjuvant therapy aiming for organ preservation is an option in selected patients.
  • Locally advanced, lower risk: more than one reasonable path, including neoadjuvant chemo with selective RT omission in carefully selected patients (PROSPECT), short- or long-course RT before TME, or TNT.
  • Higher risk: total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT), meaning chemo and radiation both before surgery. Long-course chemoRT is particularly useful for a threatened MRF, T4, a bulky or low tumor, high-risk nodal disease, or when organ preservation is a priority.
  • MMR-deficient: checkpoint immunotherapy can produce complete responses and may spare RT and surgery; this is usually managed at experienced centers.
Lower-risk locally advanced
Less intensive options

Mid/upper tumor, clear MRF, no EMVI, limited nodes. Selective RT omission or a single neoadjuvant modality may be appropriate.

Higher risk
TNT

T4, threatened MRF, EMVI, bulky or lateral nodes, low tumor. TNT, often with long-course chemoRT, then restage.

Watch-and-wait is not "no surgery because the MRI looks better"

It is a structured nonoperative management strategy for carefully selected patients with a clinical complete response after neoadjuvant therapy (judged by exam, endoscopy, and MRI), with intensive surveillance at experienced centers and TME if the tumor regrows. Patients with residual disease go to TME.

  • Target: the tumor, the entire mesorectum, and the presacral and internal iliac/obturator nodes; add external iliac nodes for anterior organ invasion and inguinal nodes when the anal canal is involved.
  • Setup: a comfortably full bladder (sometimes prone) pushes small bowel out of the pelvis. OARs: small bowel, bladder, femoral heads.
RAPIDO & PRODIGE 23

Moving chemotherapy before surgery (TNT) reduced treatment failure (RAPIDO) and improved survival (PRODIGE 23) in high-risk disease.

OPRA

After TNT, about half of patients kept their rectum with watch-and-wait, supporting organ preservation as a planned goal.

Paradigm 3: Esophageal Cancer: Neoadjuvant or Definitive

1
Early superficial

T1a: endoscopic therapy for appropriate lesions. Deeper early tumors without nodes usually go to surgery.

2
Resectable, locally advanced

Neoadjuvant therapy → esophagectomy. The exact choice depends on histology, location, surgical fitness, and the systemic therapy strategy.

3
Definitive

Definitive chemoRT, especially for cervical tumors, unresectable disease, patients unfit for surgery, and selected SCC.

  • Histology shapes the neoadjuvant choice. For SCC, neoadjuvant chemoRT remains a major standard. For resectable esophageal and GEJ adenocarcinoma, perioperative systemic therapy has become increasingly important. The final choice is a multidisciplinary decision.
  • SCC is more radiosensitive and more often has a complete pathologic response, which is why definitive chemoRT (with surgery held for residual or recurrent disease) is reasonable in selected SCC patients.
  • Patients with residual disease after neoadjuvant chemoRT and surgery may receive adjuvant immunotherapy.
  • Planning: long target volumes (see Anatomy), 4D-CT for distal tumors. OARs: lungs and heart above all (lung dose matters for postoperative complications), plus cord, and liver, stomach, and kidneys for distal tumors.
CROSS

Preoperative chemoRT before esophagectomy improved survival over surgery alone, establishing trimodality therapy as a major pathway.

Paradigm 4: Pancreatic Cancer: Systemic Therapy First, RT Selected

Resectable
Systemic therapy + surgery

Whipple (head) or distal pancreatectomy, with adjuvant chemotherapy; neoadjuvant chemo is increasingly used. Routine adjuvant chemoRT is controversial.

Borderline
Neoadjuvant

Neoadjuvant systemic therapy ± RT (chemoRT or SBRT) → restaging → surgery if feasible.

Locally advanced
Systemic therapy first

Selected patients without progression may receive chemoRT or SBRT for local control, especially when local progression threatens symptoms or survival.

  • The role of radiation in pancreatic cancer is selective and still evolving; chemotherapy remains the backbone because most patients' risk is distant spread.
  • SBRT is limited by the duodenum, stomach, and bowel wrapped around the pancreas (bleeding, ulcer, perforation).
  • Radiation also palliates pain, including celiac plexus pain.
PRODIGE 24

Adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX improved survival after resection, showing that effective systemic therapy drives outcomes in pancreatic cancer.

Paradigm 5: Liver (HCC): The Liver Is the OAR

Every HCC decision balances tumor control against preserving enough functioning liver.

SituationUsual options
Potentially curable, localizedTransplant, resection, or ablation
Liver-confined, not a surgery or ablation candidateTACE, Y-90 radioembolization, or SBRT in selected patients
AdvancedSystemic therapy
Portal vein tumor thrombus or special anatomySelected liver-directed RT approaches, alongside systemic therapy
  • SBRT also serves as a bridge to transplant.
  • Liver radiation is generally reserved for patients with good liver function (usually Child-Pugh A, selected B). The feared toxicity is radiation-induced liver disease and loss of liver function.
Planning details: liver constraints▾
  • A common SBRT goal is to keep at least about 700 cc of uninvolved liver below 15 Gy (in 3-5 fractions), plus mean liver dose limits that depend on fractionation and liver function.
  • Nearby stomach, duodenum, and bowel often limit the dose more than the liver itself; central tumors near the hilum risk biliary stricture.
RTOG 1112

Adding SBRT to sorafenib improved outcomes in unresectable HCC, supporting a selected role for liver SBRT.

Paradigm 6: Stomach: Surgery and Systemic Therapy First

  • Surgery + perioperative systemic therapy are the backbone; the regimen depends on resectability, histology, biomarkers, and contemporary systemic therapy.
  • Radiation is selective: some postoperative situations (positive margins or inadequate nodal surgery, especially without preoperative therapy) and palliation of bleeding, pain, or obstruction.

Paradigm 7: Radiation Is Not Only Curative

1
Bleeding

Hemostatic RT for gastric, rectal, or other GI bleeding, often in a short course.

2
Obstruction

RT in selected patients, alongside stents or surgical diversion (dysphagia, rectal obstruction).

3
Pain

Pancreatic and celiac plexus pain, pelvic pain, liver capsule pain.

4
Oligometastases

Selected SBRT to limited liver or lung metastases when surgery or ablation isn't suitable.

How I Plan a GI Radiation Case

  1. Define the target: the primary tumor, the regional nodes at risk, or the postoperative bed.
  2. Understand motion: the distal esophagus, GEJ, stomach, pancreas, and liver move with breathing → 4D-CT, breath hold, abdominal compression, or fiducials. Pelvic targets move with bladder and rectal filling.
  3. Identify the site-specific OARs (table below).
  4. Choose the technique: IMRT/VMAT for most curative cases, SBRT for selected small targets, with daily image guidance (IGRT).
  5. Anticipate toxicity and plan supportive care before day 1.

Trials: Deeper Dive

The trials a Sub-I needs are already in each paradigm above, one or two per disease. The box below has the numbers and the other trials you'll hear named on service.

Trial details and additional trials (optional)▾
  • CROSS: 41.4 Gy with weekly carboplatin/paclitaxel before surgery; pathologic complete response about 29% overall and about 49% in SCC; median survival nearly doubled.
  • ACT II: many complete responses only seen at about 26 weeks. RTOG 9811: mitomycin-based chemoRT beat cisplatin induction.
  • German CAO/ARO/AIO-94: preoperative chemoRT beat postoperative chemoRT for local control with less toxicity, same survival.
  • RAPIDO: the 5-year update showed more locoregional recurrence with short-course TNT, so many favor long-course chemoRT for a threatened MRF or T4.
  • PROSPECT: for selected mid/upper locally advanced tumors, FOLFOX with chemoRT only for poor responders was noninferior to routine chemoRT.
  • Cercek (dostarlimab): in MMR-deficient locally advanced rectal cancer, PD-1 blockade alone produced complete clinical responses in essentially all patients treated.
  • RTOG 8501: chemoRT beat RT alone for esophageal cancer. RTOG 9405: 64.8 Gy was no better than 50.4 Gy.
  • ESOPEC: for resectable esophageal adenocarcinoma, perioperative FLOT improved survival over CROSS. CheckMate 577: adjuvant nivolumab for residual disease after neoadjuvant chemoRT and surgery.
  • PRODIGE 24: median overall survival about 54 vs 35 months with mFOLFIRINOX vs gemcitabine. LAP07: chemoRT after chemo improved local control but not survival in locally advanced disease. PREOPANC: supported neoadjuvant chemoRT in resectable and borderline disease.
  • INT-0116: adjuvant chemoRT after mostly limited gastric node dissection improved survival. CRITICS: after periop chemo and adequate surgery, adding postoperative chemoRT did not help.

GI guidelines (NCCN and ASTRO) are changing quickly, especially for rectal, anal, and pancreatic cancer, so check the current versions for real patients.

Putting It Together: Three Consults

GI is too varied for one case, so here are three short consults. Answer each question before opening it.

Consult 1: Rectum

A 58-year-old has a low rectal adenocarcinoma. MRI: T3b N1, EMVI positive, tumor 1 mm from the mesorectal fascia. CT shows no metastases.

Why does this patient need a pelvic MRI before anything else?▾

MRI defines T, Margin, and Spread plus height, which is what decides the neoadjuvant plan. CT cannot judge the mesorectal fascia.

Is this lower or higher risk?▾

Higher risk: a threatened MRF (≤1 mm), EMVI, nodal disease, and a low tumor. Check MMR status, since MMR deficiency would change the plan.

What neoadjuvant approach fits, and why long-course RT?▾

TNT, typically with long-course chemoRT: it gives more tumor shrinkage away from a threatened margin, and in a low tumor it maximizes the chance of a complete response and organ preservation.

After TNT, the restaging MRI and endoscopy show no residual tumor. Surgery or watch-and-wait?▾

With a true clinical complete response, a structured watch-and-wait program with intensive surveillance is reasonable at an experienced center; TME is done if the tumor regrows. With residual disease, the patient goes to TME (likely an APR given the height).

Consult 2: Anus

A 52-year-old has a 3 cm anal canal mass and a suspicious left inguinal node.

What is it most likely, and how is it staged?▾

Anal squamous cell carcinoma (HPV-driven). Biopsy the mass, sample the node, and get MRI, CT ± PET/CT, and HIV testing. A 3 cm tumor is T2; an involved inguinal node is N1a.

What is the treatment, and why not an upfront APR?▾

Definitive chemoRT with 5-FU (or capecitabine) and mitomycin, IMRT to the primary, pelvic nodes, and groins, with a higher dose to the involved node. ChemoRT cures most patients and preserves the sphincter (Nigro, ACT II); APR would mean a permanent colostomy without improving cure.

Eight weeks after treatment there is still a small palpable abnormality. What now?▾

If it's regressing, keep watching: anal cancer responds slowly, over months (up to about 26 weeks). Biopsy only for persistent or progressive disease; biopsy-proven persistence goes to salvage APR.

Consult 3: Pancreas

A 67-year-old has a pancreatic head adenocarcinoma with 90° of contact with the SMA, no venous involvement, and no metastases.

Resectable, borderline, or locally advanced?▾

Borderline resectable: SMA contact ≤180°. Any arterial contact means it isn't straightforwardly resectable; >180° would be locally advanced.

What comes first, and where might radiation fit?▾

Neoadjuvant systemic therapy, then restaging. Radiation (chemoRT or SBRT) may be added in selected patients to improve the chance of a negative margin, followed by surgery if feasible. Its exact role is still debated, so this is a multidisciplinary decision.

If SBRT is used, which organ most limits the dose?▾

The duodenum, which wraps the pancreatic head (with the stomach and bowel nearby). Too much dose risks ulcer, bleeding, or perforation.

High-Yield Summary
  • Anal cancer is treated with definitive chemoradiation with 5-FU or capecitabine and mitomycin, and surgery is mainly for biopsy-proven persistent or recurrent disease.
  • Rectal cancer treatment is risk-adapted, with total neoadjuvant therapy for higher-risk disease and selective radiation omission for carefully selected lower-risk patients.
  • Watch-and-wait is a structured nonoperative strategy for a clinical complete response, with intensive surveillance at an experienced center.
  • Esophageal cancer is treated with neoadjuvant therapy before esophagectomy or with definitive chemoradiation, especially for cervical, unresectable, or selected squamous cancers.
  • Pancreatic cancer starts with systemic therapy and resectability, and liver SBRT for HCC must protect enough functioning liver.
